title: Cluny (910)
hook: a monastery freed from local lords so its monks could pray, and a renewal that spread

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloister, the covered walk at a monastery's heart. Your line was bells and bread. Today, one monastery's freedom.

A duke has land he loves: woods, a river, a lodge where he keeps his hunting dogs. A monk asks him for it. There's a story people tell about that conversation: the duke protests that the place is full of his hounds, and the monk answers, more or less, drive out the dogs and bring in the monks. Whether or not it went that way, the duke said yes. Then he signed a charter that did something stranger than giving land away. He promised never to take it back. The place was Cluny.
screen: `A DUKE AND HIS HUNTING LODGE.` → `DRIVE OUT THE DOGS.` → `A PROMISE NEVER TO TAKE IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Here was the problem. A lord who founded a monastery could treat it as his own property: name the abbot, take the rents, lean on it when he needed money. The prayer went on, but someone else held the keys. Duke William's charter changed that. He gave Cluny to the apostles Peter and Paul and placed it under the protection of the pope in Rome. The monks, the charter says, are to be under no one's yoke: not his, not his family's, not any earthly power. No prince, no count, no bishop, not even the pope himself, may seize their goods or set an abbot over them against their will. When their abbot, Berno, died, the monks would choose the next one themselves, by the Rule of Saint Benedict. The freedom wasn't for its own sake. Cluny gave itself to the work of God: long, sung prayer through the day and night, for the living and the dead. Saint Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stand fast, and be not held again under the yoke of bondage." The charter speaks the same language of yokes. Then it spread. Other houses asked Cluny's abbots to reform them, or were handed over to Cluny, and its way of life went with them. Some later monks thought Cluny had grown too grand. But the charter's idea outlived the argument: a house of prayer should belong to God, not to whoever owns the land. Free to pray.
screen: `A LORD COULD OWN A MONASTERY.` · `UNDER NO ONE'S YOKE.` · `FREEDOM FOR THE WORK OF GOD.` · `A RENEWAL SPREADS.` · then, large: `FREE TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow's first quiet minutes, the ones the phone or the inbox usually takes, and give them a little charter of your own: phone in another room, door closed. If you pray, that's where prayer can live; if you don't, let those minutes simply be yours, unclaimed.
Cluny. A monastery whose founder signed away every claim on it, so its monks could choose their abbot and give themselves to prayer. Today's word.
Your line: free to pray. Next, the Church tries to make peace without an army. Day seven hundred ninety-eight, done.

howItsDone: Benedictine houses today, including those that trace their customs to Cluny, elect their own abbots or abbesses under the Rule of Saint Benedict and keep the hours of prayer as the center of the day.

notes: Week-end day (798): the review looks back over days 792–798 briefly.
The 'drive out the dogs and bring in the monks' exchange between Berno and Duke William is a later legend; it is told as 'a story people tell'. Confirm framing.

Charter paraphrased: gift to Peter and Paul; under papal protection (tuitio); monks under no one's yoke, including the duke's family and royal power; no prince, count, bishop or the Roman pontiff may seize goods or impose a prelate; free election after Berno's death under the Rule. Confirm.
'Some later monks thought Cluny had grown too grand' alludes to Cistercian criticism (Bernard's Apologia) and sets up day 801; confirm fairness.
